about: Reference list /grammar/phrasal-verbs-list (English: phrasal verbs). items: [phrasal verb, forms (past simple · past participle), example, level]; a string starting with '# ' is a sub-heading. Section ids are kept from the German list: trennbar = separable (object can go in the middle), untrennbar = inseparable (object after the particle), beides = no object; three-part is new. Examples in the separable section use a pronoun object where they are short, so the particle has exactly one place (the worksheet builds sentences from them). *…* in regel becomes bold.
title: Phrasal verbs
metaTitle: Phrasal verbs list: separable, inseparable and three-part, with examples – Reference – icanspeak Spanish
description: Common English phrasal verbs with past simple, past participle and an example: where the object goes, which ones never split, and three-part verbs like look forward to.
lead: Common phrasal verbs, each with its past forms and an example. The big question is where the object goes: the rule is above each list.
practice: Verb prefixes: over-, under-, out-, re-

sections.name: Separable: the object can go in the middle
sections.what: These have an object. A noun object can go before or after the particle; a pronoun (it, them, me) must go in the middle.
regel: Noun object: two places: *Turn off the light. / Turn the light off.*
Pronoun object: only in the middle: *Turn it off.* (not *Turn off it*)
A long object usually goes after the particle: *Pick up all the books on the floor.*
The verb changes, the particle doesn't: *picks up, picked up, picking up.*
Typical particles: *up, down, on, off, in, out, away, back.*
items: I'll pick you up at the station.
I turned it off and went to bed.
Could you switch it off, please?
She put it on and left.
I took them off at the door.
Can you fill it in for me?
Can you write it down for me?
I'll look it up in the dictionary.
I'll call you back in five minutes.
She gave it back to me.
Can you find out when the train leaves?
They offered her the job, but she turned it down.
Let's put it off until next week.
Don't worry, we'll sort it out.

sections.name: Inseparable: the object comes after
sections.what: These have an object too, but it always comes after the particle, even a pronoun: look after them.
regel: The object always goes after the particle: *I look after my little brother.*
Pronouns too: *I look after him.* (not *I look him after*)
Many are a verb + preposition with a special meaning: *come across* (find by chance), *get over* (feel better after).
In questions the particle stays with the verb: *Who is looking after the kids?*
items: We got on the bus in the town centre.
Get off at the next stop.
She got over her cold quickly.
I came across an old photo.
I ran into Tom at the supermarket.

sections.name: No object
sections.what: These have no object, so the verb and the particle stay together.
regel: No object, so nothing goes in the middle: *I get up at seven.*
Many are about daily routines and changes: *wake up, get up, go out, sit down, grow up.*
Some also have an object, with another meaning: *The plane took off* (left the ground) / *Take off your coat.*
They have no passive: *The car broke down.* (not *was broken down*)
items: Our car broke down on the motorway.
We set off early in the morning.
He turned up an hour late.
Slow down! You're driving too fast.

sections.name: Three-part phrasal verbs
sections.what: Verb + particle + preposition. Never split them; the object comes at the end.
regel: The object goes at the end: *I'm looking forward to the weekend.*
After the preposition use a noun, a pronoun or -ing: *I'm looking forward to seeing you.* (not *to see you*)
Many have a two-part partner: *The milk has run out.* / *We've run out of milk.*
items: looked forward to · looked forward to
I'm looking forward to the holidays.
got on with · got on with
I get on well with my sister. (US: get along with)
ran out of · run out of
put up with · put up with
I can't put up with this noise.
came up with · come up with
She came up with a great idea.
caught up with · caught up with
Go ahead, I'll catch up with you.
cut down on · cut down on
I'm trying to cut down on sugar.
kept up with · kept up with
It's hard to keep up with the news.
